fit_paragraphs.text: My work on how blind screen-reader users verify LLM answers [lib:cv] connects directly to Prof. Azenkot's empirical study of how blind and low-vision people use AI-powered scene description tools [paper:W4396833521]. Both projects use qualitative and diary-study methods with BLV participants to surface breakdowns in AI-mediated information access. SourceSpeak, my first-authored submission on non-visual provenance cues [lib:cv], extends that empirical foundation into interface design—an arc that matches the accessible information access theme Prof. Azenkot pursues at Cornell Tech [advisor:Shiri Azenkot]. I would want to work with her on empirically grounded, prototype-driven research into AI interfaces for BLV users.

Prof. Zhou's work measuring how LLMs' reluctance to express uncertainty damages user decision-making [paper:W4402671787] is the NLP-side diagnosis of the problem I approached from the interface side: users cannot tell when a model is wrong. Her interaction-centered framework for quantifying human reliance on language models [paper:W4411119305] offers methodological scaffolding I want to apply in accessibility contexts—specifically, whether provenance cues reduce miscalibrated reliance among blind users. My SourceSpeak within-subjects study [lib:cv] is a first step; a PhD with Prof. Zhou would let me connect that HCI prototype work to rigorous reliance measurement at scale.

My Microsoft Research Asia study found that family-initiated error repair doubled older adults' continued use of conversational agents over four weeks [lib:cv]—evidence that trust repair is social. Prof. Vashistha's finding that AI writing suggestions homogenize text toward Western styles [paper:W4409746764] points to a parallel asymmetry I observed in Chinese household contexts: agent defaults assume literacy and interaction norms that many older Mandarin speakers do not share [lib:interests]. His active lab and work across marginalized-community HCI [advisor:Aditya Vashistha] make him a natural collaborator for extending my older-adult conversational-agent research into cross-cultural and equity-centered directions.

Prof. Fussell's deployment of a fact-checking chatbot in private messaging groups [paper:W4406258040] maps closely onto the trust and error-repair dynamics I documented with older adults and conversational agents in Chinese households [lib:cv]. Her study of parasocial relationships formed through AI-simulated voice messages [paper:W4410513031] raises exactly the questions I encountered about emotional attachment and continued use after agent errors. Her long focus on cross-cultural computer-mediated communication [advisor:Susan R. Fussell] would ground my second research thread—older adults, family mediation, and conversational agents—in a richer theoretical framework.

sop.text:
In a diary study with 14 blind screen-reader users, I asked how they verify LLM answers [lib:cv]. The most common strategy was asking a sighted friend—exactly the dependence these tools were supposed to remove [lib:sop_draft]. That finding drove SourceSpeak, a browser plug-in that reads answer provenance aloud [lib:cv]. In a within-subjects study (n = 12), participants caught 2.3 times more incorrect AI answers than without it [lib:cv]. The result is the core of my first-authored submission, "SourceSpeak: Non-Visual Provenance Cues for LLM Answers," currently under review [lib:cv].

A second thread emerged during my research internship at Microsoft Research Asia (June–August 2026), where I ran a conversational-agent study with 20 older adults (ages 65–82) and their adult children [lib:cv]. When a family member initiated the repair after an agent error, continued use over four weeks doubled [lib:cv]. The takeaway: trust in AI agents is repaired socially, not just technically [lib:sop_draft]. That study produced a co-authored workshop paper and pushed me toward a second research question—how do cultural context, family structure, and interaction design together shape whether marginalized users stay with or abandon AI tools [lib:interests]?

These two threads share a common structure: a population excluded from mainstream AI design (blind users, older adults in Chinese households), an AI interface that produces errors, and a design intervention that changes how those errors are surfaced and recovered. In a PhD I want to build that into a research program: mixed-methods studies that document breakdown, followed by prototype-driven experiments that test repairs, feeding back into theory about legibility, trust, and inclusion [lib:interests].

Cornell's Information Science program is where I want to pursue this. Prof. Shiri Azenkot's empirical work on AI-powered scene description for blind and low-vision users [paper:W4396833521] addresses the same breakdowns I observed in SourceSpeak but from an applications perspective; working with her would let me combine my provenance-cue approach with her broader empirical program on accessible information access [advisor:Shiri Azenkot]. Prof. Kaitlyn Zhou's framework for measuring human reliance on language models [paper:W4411119305] and her study of how LLMs' reluctance to express uncertainty harms decisions [paper:W4402671787] offer methodological grounding I need to move from prototype studies to rigorous reliance measurement—her NLP+HCI methods are a direct complement to my HCI-first approach. Prof. Aditya Vashistha's finding that AI writing suggestions homogenize text toward Western styles [paper:W4409746764] is a cross-cultural asymmetry parallel to what I observed in Chinese household conversational-agent use; his active lab [advisor:Aditya Vashistha] and focus on marginalized communities would support the older-adult thread of my work. And Prof. Susan Fussell's deployment of a fact-checking chatbot in private messaging groups [paper:W4406258040] maps directly onto the trust and error-repair dynamics I documented at MSRA.

I bring to this program a ranked undergraduate record at Tsinghua (GPA 3.86/4.0, rank 9/180) [lib:cv], two years of active research producing a first-authored submission and a workshop paper [lib:cv], screen-reader testing experience with both NVDA and VoiceOver [lib:cv], and sustained community work at the Beijing Blind Technology Center [lib:cv]. The Tsinghua Outstanding Undergraduate Research Award in 2026 recognized the SourceSpeak project [lib:cv]. My goal is a faculty position or senior research role where I can continue designing and evaluating interfaces that make AI legible to users left out of the design process [lib:sop_draft].

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student interested in BLV users and LLM interfaces
emails.body:
Dear Prof. Azenkot,

I am a final-year B.Eng. student at Tsinghua University applying to Cornell's Information Science PhD program for Fall 2027 [lib:profile]. My research focuses on how blind screen-reader users verify LLM-generated answers and on interface designs that expose answer provenance non-visually [lib:interests]. I built SourceSpeak, a plug-in that reads provenance cues aloud; in a within-subjects study (n = 12), participants caught 2.3 times more incorrect AI answers, and I am the first author of a paper currently under review [lib:cv].

I read your 2024 CHI paper "Investigating Use Cases of AI-Powered Scene Description Applications for Blind and Low Vision People" [paper:W4396833521] and found the empirical breakdown of use cases and failure modes directly relevant to my own diary-study findings. I would be very interested in pursuing similar questions in your lab.

Are you taking PhD students for Fall 2027? I am happy to share my CV and writing sample.

Sincerely,
Mei Lin

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student — human reliance on LLMs and accessibility
emails.body:

I am a final-year B.Eng. student at Tsinghua University working at the intersection of HCI and LLM reliability, specifically on how blind screen-reader users detect incorrect AI answers [lib:interests]. My first-authored paper on SourceSpeak—a plug-in delivering non-visual provenance cues that tripled error detection in a within-subjects study—is currently under review [lib:cv].

Your 2025 NAACL paper "REL-A.I.: An Interaction-Centered Approach To Measuring Human-LM Reliance" [paper:W4411119305] directly addresses the reliance calibration questions I want to pursue in a PhD. My prototype work suggests provenance cues shift reliance, but I lack the measurement framework your paper proposes; I would like to build on it in accessibility contexts.

I would appreciate knowing whether you are accepting PhD students for Fall 2027. I am glad to send my CV.

Sincerely,
Mei Lin
